title: Doriscus assembled nations
contributors: Herodotus names Persian, Median, Anatolian, Egyptian, Arabian, Indian, Central Asian, and other infantry and cavalry contingents with different equipment
command_link: National contingents appear under named commanders; Herodotus then names senior Persian commanders over the infantry
battlefield_function: Infantry and cavalry traditions remained visible rather than becoming one equipment system
supply_support: The baggage train and beasts passed first; Herodotus says the picked Persian corps carried food separately from the rest
coordination_test: The host is first described as mixed together and then marshalled by nations at Doriscus
reported_anchor: A later editorial count finds 61 people-labels: 46 infantry, 8 cavalry, and 12 naval; categories overlap
interpretation: The catalogue makes imperial military plurality legible and also exposes the work of turning named contingents into an army.
limits: The 61 labels are an editorial count of Herodotus's catalogue and are not headcounts shares or proof that every listed formation fought as described.

title: Supply was staged before the march
contributors: Transport ships and local staging zones moved grain ahead of Xerxes's advance
command_link: Herodotus describes the work as distributed among those responsible for carrying stores
battlefield_function: Five named depot zones positioned grain along the route before the army arrived
supply_support: Stores were sent to Leuce Acte, Tyrodiza, Doriscus, Eion on the Strymon, and Macedonia; a market operated at Doriscus
coordination_test: A coalition could not simply converge: food had to be placed across the route before the mass arrived
interpretation: Advance preparation connected maritime transport local storage and the marching army.
limits: Herodotus gives no surviving quantities depot capacities delivery cadence spoilage rate or proof that these five zones describe the entire supply system.

title: The fleet borrowed maritime systems
contributors: Phoenician and Syrian-Palestinian, Egyptian, Cypriot, Cilician, Pamphylian, Lycian, Carian, Ionian, Aeolian, Hellespontine, and island contingents appear in Herodotus's fleet list
command_link: Local contingents retained named leaders while royal relatives and senior nobles occupied higher command
battlefield_function: Sailing, rowing, ship handling, and marine fighting drew on distinct coastal traditions and equipment
supply_support: The fleet moved beside a coastal campaign and helped carry supplies as well as combatants
coordination_test: Naval capacity came from regional maritime institutions the inland court could command but did not replace
reported_anchor: 12 naval peoples in the How and Wells editorial count; no ancient ship total is accepted here
interpretation: The imperial fleet was a coalition of existing maritime capacities rather than a standardized Persian navy.
limits: Herodotus's ship totals and judgments about relative seamanship are not converted into fleet size survival rate or national effectiveness scores.

title: Cunaxa exposed the command interface
source_class: eyewitness Greek narrative plus scholarly reconstruction
contributors: Cyrus combined Greek hoplites and peltasts with Persian infantry, armored cavalry, other horsemen, and chariots
command_link: Cyrus held the center, Clearchus the river-side Greek right, and Ariaeus the left; an order to attack the royal center reportedly passed through an interpreter
battlefield_function: The intended plan paired a Greek heavy-infantry strike with Cyrus's cavalry attack on Artaxerxes
supply_support: Xenophon reports four hundred wagons of flour and wine prepared for crisis distribution and later pillaged
coordination_test: Clearchus kept the Greek right by the river and pursued the opposing left instead of wheeling toward the royal center; Cyrus's attack then became isolated
reported_anchor: 400 provision wagons reported by Xenophon; no total army figure used
interpretation: A coalition could win local fights yet fail strategically when its command interfaces did not produce the intended sequence.
limits: Xenophon was a participant but not present at every command exchange; the interpreter episode tactical reconstruction and reported wagon count remain literary evidence.

title: Gaugamela arranged a coalition by role
source_class: later Greek campaign narrative claiming an earlier written order
contributors: The reported wings and center combine Bactrian, Dahae, Arachosian, Persian, Susian, Cadusian, Syrian, Mesopotamian, Median, Parthian, Sacae, Armenian, Cappadocian, Indian, Carian, Mardian, Babylonian, and Greek formations
command_link: Bessus held the left, Mazaeus the right, and Darius the royal center; regional commanders linked contingents to those command zones
battlefield_function: Cavalry concentrated on the wings; guards, archers, infantry, and Greek mercenaries protected the center; chariots were placed forward
supply_support: The ground was reportedly levelled for cavalry and chariots, but Arrian preserves no Persian provisioning ledger for the battle
coordination_test: Arrian says Aristobulus traced the arrangement to a captured written scheme, yet the surviving narrative was composed centuries later
reported_anchor: 3 command zones: Bessus left, Darius center, Mazaeus right; no force total used
interpretation: The order of battle shows regional forces nested into an imperial tactical design rather than homogenized.
limits: Arrian's huge force totals are excluded; the captured-document claim order details and battlefield sequence remain a later Greek narrative based on lost sources.

title: Administration made movement repeatable
contributors: Officials, messengers, travelers, workers, animals, storeroom managers, and commodity carriers appear in the surviving regional records
command_link: Sealed authorizations, local offices, road-station vouchers, and central accounting connected movement to royal administration
battlefield_function: This is logistical infrastructure rather than a battlefield formation
supply_support: The archive records food distribution, transport, state reserves, fodder, and en-route provisioning from storerooms
coordination_test: The records show a reusable provisioning substrate but do not document Xerxes's whole campaign or every imperial army
reported_anchor: Regional archive window; no campaign headcount or ration total inferred
interpretation: Coalition warfare rested on administrative routines that moved authorization food animals and people before battle.
limits: The Persepolis Fortification archive is regional unevenly preserved and not an army supply ledger or empire-wide logistics census.
